Advanced RAG Demo

Multimodal retrieval for complex technical PDFs: merged-cell tables, footnoted spec sheets, charts and rotated engineering drawings, with exact citations and the source image next to every answer.
Prepared by
Vjenceslav Nadinic
Claude Sonnet / Opus on Amazon BedrockAmazon OpenSearch ServerlessStrands AgentsAWS CDK
Sample document: Daikin Mega-Q Engineering Data EDUS342358A, a public 36-page engineering data book
Welcome. This deck walks through a proof of concept for RAG over hard technical PDFs: what makes them hard, the architecture on AWS, how the custom parser works, what we measured, and how it was built. Everything shown uses a public engineering data book from Daikin; no customer data.
The problem

Basic RAG breaks on engineering documents

The answers live in grids, footnotes and drawings. Plain text extraction flattens or loses exactly those.

Merged-cell tables

"How many units for 10,000 gal/day at 23 °F?" The answer is one merged cell spanning five columns.

7.9 k 8.5 k 9.0 k 9.5 k 10.0 k … 4 5 6 7 4 5 6 7 4 5 6 7 ← which column is 10.0 k?

Footnoted spec sheets

"What is the winter COP?" The value is in a spec row; its rating conditions are in a ★2 footnote at the bottom of the page.

COP 3.5 ★2 … (200 lines later) \uf048 2 Outside air 44.6°F DB … ← glyph is a private-use char

Drawings and charts

Wiring and dimension drawings are printed sideways; charts are raster images. Their numbers are not in the text layer at all.

(no text) (no text) ← the whole chart is a picture
Three failure modes. Merged cells: text extraction gives you a row of numbers without the spans, so you can't tell which column a value belongs to. Footnotes: the condition that makes a value meaningful sits far away, and Daikin even encodes the star as a private-use glyph. Drawings and charts: rotated or rasterised, so there's simply no text to extract.
The idea

Explode once, stitch for every question

Parsing takes each page apart into typed elements. Retrieval puts the right pieces back together. One ID connects both directions.

The core mental model. RAG isn't "a vector database"; it's a set of parts connected by IDs. Parsing runs once per document and explodes each page. Retrieval runs per question and stitches the relevant pieces back together. The element_id is what makes both directions line up.

Concept sketch on a public Daikin drive manual (IM 1190-3, pp. 39–41). The build refined it: tables stay whole in the knowledge base with the PDF's own grid as the source of truth; exact lookups over structured data come later as a text-to-SQL tool.
This is the original concept we started from, on a different public Daikin manual. The idea: don't chunk pages blindly; decide per region what it is and where it should live. Parent chunks for the section, image plus a description for diagrams, structured records for parameter rows, vector chunks for descriptions, and cross-reference metadata so the agent can follow "see parameter 1103". The build kept the spirit and simplified the plumbing, as the next slides show.
Architecture

End to end on AWS

Built · parserDesigned · knowledge base, agent, UILater phases
Top lane is ingestion: PDFs into a parser that uses Claude on Bedrock only where needed, writing chunks and metadata, full elements and images to S3. A Bedrock Knowledge Base ingests the chunks as-is (chunking NONE) into OpenSearch Serverless with hybrid search, because model numbers and drawing numbers need exact keyword matches. Bottom lane is the question path: React and Cloudscape, a thin FastAPI backend, and a Strands agent on AgentCore Runtime. Solid green is built today; dashed orange is designed; the dotted row is the later phases.
Built
Parser

Four passes, and only one of them calls a model

Read what the PDF already knows before paying for vision. Pages run in parallel (concurrency 5).

1
Deterministic

Prepare

  • Text layer with position, font, direction
  • Clean quirks: control chars, full-width digits, private-use ★ glyphs
  • Running headers and footers detected
  • Chapter › section breadcrumb per page
  • Triage signals → route per page
2
The only model calls

Extract

  • T0 text pages: own code + PDF table grids
  • T1 visual pages: Claude Sonnet vision
  • Exact PDF values sent as anchors
  • Every value checked against the PDF
  • T2 failing pages retried with Claude Opus
3
Deterministic

Assemble

  • Stable element IDs in reading order
  • Tables continued on the next page merged
  • Footnotes resolved into the rows that cite them
  • Model and drawing numbers collected
  • Crops snapped to PDF coordinates
4
Deterministic

Write

  • One chunk per element or part
  • Metadata file per chunk for filtering
  • Full element stored for small-to-big
  • Page images + crops
  • Manifest: routes, tokens, timings
Four passes. Prepare, Assemble and Write are deterministic: PyMuPDF plus our own code. Only Extract calls Claude, and only for pages that need vision. Every pass writes inspectable output, so you can see exactly why a page went where it went.
Built · real run
Pass 1 · triage

The right effort for every page

A few measurable signals pick the route before any model call. Hover a page to see why.

pseudo-coderoute(page): if no text and no image and no drawing: return SKIP if image coverage ≥ 15% or drawing items ≥ 60 or rotated text ≥ 25% or printable < 90% or table with merged cells / > 120 cells or < 200 chars next to visual content: return T1 # Claude Sonnet vision return T0 # text layer only, no model# T2 (Claude Opus) is never chosen here:# a page only gets there by failing a T1 check

Blank pages are skipped. Pages with images, many vector drawing items, rotated text, merged-cell tables or very little text next to visuals go to vision. Everything else is read straight from the PDF. Thresholds live in a per-family profile.

Thresholds live in a per-family profile (YAML), calibrated on this sample. Same engine, different document families.

SKIP · 3T0 text · 7 T1 Sonnet · 24T2 Opus escalation · 2
Here's the real run on all 36 pages. Three blank pages skipped, seven clean text pages read without any model, 24 sent to Sonnet vision, and two escalated to Opus after failing a check: page 5 on a number mismatch, page 6 on schema. Hover any page for its actual triage reasons.
Built
Pass 2 · extract

Vision, but trust nothing it can't prove

The model copies from what the PDF already contains, answers through one fixed schema, and every number is checked.

pseudo-coderesult = sonnet(upright_image, anchors, pdf_grids, schema_tool)for table in result.tables: overwrite cells from pdf_gridif not (schema_ok and sane and number_match ≥ 0.90): result = better_of(result, opus(…, effort="high"))bad AWS setup (no access, wrong model id) → stop after 1 call

Cost control built in: the first vision page runs alone to warm the prompt cache (220k cached input tokens reused), and a missing permission stops the run after one call instead of failing every page.

The vision lane. We never ask the model to read from scratch: it gets the upright page, the exact strings from the text layer with positions, and for vector tables the exact grid from PDF. Output goes through one tool with a fixed schema. Then four checks; the number guard is the important one. Failures go to Opus with higher effort. In the full run, only two pages needed Opus, and both passed.
Built · measured
What the experiments showed

For tables, the PDF grid beats the model's eyes

merged cell → 5 systems

Golden question: "How many systems for 10,000 gal/day at 23 °F?" Column 10.0 k sits inside one cell merged across five columns (9.5 k–11.6 k).

Rendering experiment (13 runs, 4 page types): full page vs. 5 tiles vs. layout-model regions. Tiles cost 1.5–4× more input tokens with no accuracy gain, so the default is the full page and the layout model dependency was dropped.

up to 13
wrong cells per table block when the model reads merged cells alone; errors sit at span boundaries and change between runs
39 / 39
cells exact from the PDF's own vector table grid (spans filled from the left neighbour)
0
wrong cells once the grid is sent as authoritative and model cells are reconciled to it
The most important finding of the build. On merged-cell selection tables, vision models are close but not exact; errors land at span boundaries and vary run to run. That's model noise, not resolution. The PDF already contains the exact grid for vector tables. So the grid is sent to the model as authoritative and any disagreeing cell is overwritten. Result: zero wrong cells. Raster-only tables keep the model result plus the number guard.
Built
Rendering details that matter

Upright pages, clean text, precise crops

crop · diagram (dimension)
↻

Rotation fixed before the model sees it

Dimension and wiring drawings are stored sideways. The renderer turns them upright and fits the long edge to the model's image budget.

✂

Crops snapped to the PDF

The model's bounding box is sanity-checked and snapped to real PDF coordinates. 63 of 86 elements got a crop; the rest fall back to the full page image.

Aa

Text the PDF hides

Control characters inside words, full-width digits (１０４ → 104) and a private-use glyph for ★ are normalised, so checks compare like with like.

≡

Running headers ignored

Lines repeating in the top or bottom 6 % of many pages are kept out of content and checks. Drawing numbers in the footer are kept.

Small things with large effects. Rotated drawings are turned upright before the model sees them. Crops are snapped to PDF coordinates so the UI can show exactly the element that was cited. And the PDF text layer is full of traps; for example, full-width digits made the number guard fail until we normalised them.

One schema for every route. 7 element types across the document: 26 diagrams, 23 tables, 17 notes, 11 text sections, 3 spec-row blocks, 3 charts, 3 photos. Each gets a stable ID: document : page : element.

Also in assembly: tables that continue on the next page are merged when headers match; footnote markers (★1…★12) are resolved into the rows that use them; model and drawing numbers are collected as identifiers.

Pass 4 · write

Every chunk stands on its own

example output · shortenedEDUS342358A › 1. Basic Information › 2. System Overview › Controller kitPage 5 · spec_rowsContext: Specifications of the Mega-Q tank controller kit BRP26B2VJU.Identifiers: BRP26B2VJU - Power supply: 208/230 V, 60 Hz- Accessories (harness length): Temperature sensor 1 (9.8 ft (3 m)); Temperature sensor 2 (14.1 ft (4.3 m)); Temperature sensor 3 (18.4 ft (5.6 m)); … Facts:- Temperature sensor 2 harness length is 14.1 ft (4.3 m).

Each chunk opens with its breadcrumb (document › chapter › section › element), page and type, a one-line context, the identifiers it contains, the content itself, and generated plain-language fact sentences.

element_idpage · page_endelement_typechapter · sectionmodels[]drawing_nopart n of mcrop imagepage imageparse route · modeldepartment · access level

Metadata file next to each chunk: used for knowledge base filters, citations and (later) per-user access.

Split rules per type

  • Text: headings → paragraphs → sentences, ~10 % overlap
  • Tables: whole if small, else row groups; header row and cited footnotes repeated in every part
  • Charts, diagrams: one chunk
  • Tiny notes: merged into their parent

Target ~650 tokens, max 1,500. Knowledge base chunking is NONE: it indexes our chunks as-is.

Why fact sentences?

"Sensor 2 harness length is 14.1 ft" matches how people ask. Table rows alone embed poorly; the sentences give the vector search something to grab.

This is a real chunk, shortened. The breadcrumb and context lines mean the chunk still makes sense when retrieved alone. Identifiers make exact model numbers searchable. Fact sentences are generated deterministically from table rows. The metadata file carries the IDs and image links, plus department and access level so per-user filtering works later without re-parsing.
Designed · spec 02–03
Retrieval

Search small, answer big

Small chunks give precise matches. The answer is built from the full element and its image.

Bedrock Retrieve · request shaperetrieve(knowledgeBaseId="<kb-id>", retrievalQuery={ text: "Which sensors come with kit BRP26B2VJU…?" }, vectorSearchConfiguration={ numberOfResults: 8, overrideSearchType: "HYBRID", filter: { andAll: [ department = "engineering", access_level in ["public", "internal"] ] } })

Why hybrid: technical questions mix meaning ("how long are the cables") with exact tokens (model and drawing numbers) that pure vector search handles poorly.

Why small-to-big: a table split into five parts is found by its best part, but the model reads the whole table.

This is the designed retrieval path, coming in specs 2 and 3. Hybrid search on the Bedrock Knowledge Base over OpenSearch Serverless: a semantic leg and a keyword leg, fused, with a metadata filter for who is asking. We keep the top two or three element IDs and load the full elements and their crops. That's the "stitch".

Built · learned
Lessons

What the runs taught us

▦

Deterministic beats probabilistic where it exists

The PDF's vector grid is exact; the model is close. Use the model to understand, the PDF to be exact.

□

Full page beats tiles

Tiles and layout-model crops cost 1.5–4× the tokens for no accuracy gain on these documents.

#

A check needs something to check against

The number guard is skipped when the text layer has fewer than 5 numbers (covers, raster charts). Otherwise it fires false alarms.

Aa

PDF text is full of traps

Control characters inside words, full-width digits, private-use glyphs, "208/230" split in two. Each one first showed up as a failed check.

⚡

Warm the cache, fail fast

Run the first vision page alone so the others hit the prompt cache; a bad credential or model ID stops the run after one call.

~

Models vary run to run

The same page escalated for schema in one run and for numbers in the next. Validation is not optional.

✎

Fill what is derivable, don't escalate

When the model omits a field we can derive (a caption from the title), repair it and log it instead of paying for Opus.

◎

Be precise about the API

Reasoning effort and structured output are set through specific request fields; a quick live spike found that before any code was built on it.

The practical lessons. The first one is the headline: wherever a deterministic source exists, use it, and let the model do what only a model can. Most others came from the full run, where the first attempt flagged five pages for review; all five were false alarms caused by PDF quirks, which were then fixed in the checks.

How it was built · 2 of 2

Prove it before you build on it

Spikes first

Measure, then design

A live API spike (effort settings, tool reliability, caching, image budget) and a 13-run rendering experiment ran before the parser was written. Their results set the defaults.

Test-first tasks

162 unit tests

Run with no AWS access and no real PDF, on synthetic PDFs generated in the tests. Plus 6 sample tests on the real document. Lint clean on every commit.

Golden set

10 real questions

Each with the expected answer and its source page and element type, written from the document before parsing. Checked after every parser change.

Human review

Side-by-side page

A generated review page shows each PDF page next to its elements and the golden questions it answers. The owner signed off on it.

Live runs

5 pages, then 36

First a 5-page live parse of the hardest page types, then the full document. Each run's surprises became fixes and tests.

Independent review

19 findings closed

A full read-only code review (3 high, 10 medium, 6 low). Every fix came with a test that fails without it.

The quality loop. We measured before designing, wrote tests with each task, and defined a golden question set up front. Unit tests need neither AWS nor the real PDF. Live runs went from five pages to the whole document, and an independent review closed the loop.
Decisions

Key decisions and why

ADR 1 · accepted

Own parser, outside the knowledge base

Built-in parsers are fixed per data source, and the only hook runs after chunking, when layout and images are already gone.

ADR 2 · accepted

OpenSearch Serverless, hybrid search

Model and drawing numbers need exact keyword matches next to semantic search.

ADR 3 · accepted

One pipeline, routed per page

Real documents mix blank, text and complex pages; a per-document choice overspends or loses charts.

ADR 6 · accepted

Element chunks, small-to-big

Page chunks mix topics; fixed-size chunks cut tables mid-row. Search parts, answer from whole elements.

Experiment · accepted

Full page + authoritative PDF grid

Measured: tiles cost more for nothing; the grid fixes merged cells exactly. Layout model dropped.

ADR 4 · accepted

AWS CDK in Python

Parser, agent and backend are Python; one language end to end.

ADR 7 · accepted

React + Cloudscape, thin FastAPI

Streaming, agent steps, sign-in and images beside citations; the browser never talks to AWS directly.

ADR 8 · accepted

Multi-user earlier

Documents are parsed once, so access metadata must exist before ingestion; tools can be user-scoped from day one.

The decisions, each with its record. The thread through all of them: keep control over the parts where accuracy is decided, use managed services everywhere else, and make choices that won't force a re-parse later.
Roadmap

From parser to a multi-user agent

Phase 1

Minimal flow

Parser done. Next: knowledge base (CDK), agent on AgentCore, React UI.

Phase 2

Live feel

Streaming answers, AgentCore Memory, AgentCore Observability.

Phase 3

Guardrails

Bedrock Guardrails: contextual grounding, PII, denied topics, prompt attacks.

Phase 3b

Multi-user

Cognito sign-in, per-user documents, data, tools and memory.

Phase 4

Tools via MCP

AgentCore Gateway: Lambda and OpenAPI targets, an existing MCP server.

Phase 4b

Text-to-SQL

Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 + Data API, row-level scoping per user.

Phase 5

Harden

Retrieval tuning, knowledge base evaluations, full infrastructure as code.

Each phase follows the same loop: requirements → design → tasks → tests and golden questions → live run → review.

Where it goes next. Phase 1 completes the minimal end-to-end flow. Then streaming and memory, guardrails with contextual grounding, multi-user identity, tools through AgentCore Gateway and MCP, a text-to-SQL tool for structured data (where the concept slide's "exact lookup" idea comes back), and finally tuning and full IaC.
Summary

Accurate RAG on hard PDFs is an engineering problem, not a model problem.

1

Spend model effort per page, not per document

2

Let the PDF be exact; let the model understand

3

Chunk by element, connect everything by ID, cite with the image

4

Specs, tests and golden questions before scale
